A2.text:
Nigar and Aysel are best friends. They first met at a university in Baku five years ago. Nigar always says Aysel is very supportive. She has complete trust in her.

Last year, Aysel moved to Sheki for a new job. At first, they talked every day. But soon, Aysel got very busy with her new office. One evening, they argued on the phone.

“You never have time for me,” Nigar said.

Aysel was angry. “I am just tired,” she said. They stopped talking for two long weeks.

Nigar felt very sad. She walked up and down Nizami Street alone. She missed her friend. One Saturday, Nigar sat in their favourite cafe near the Boulevard. She ordered tea, but felt lonely. She looked at her phone. She wanted to call Aysel and say sorry.

Suddenly, someone touched her shoulder. She looked up. It was Aysel, holding a box of sweets!

“I took the morning bus from Sheki,” Aysel said. “I am so sorry. I really missed you.”

Nigar smiled and stood up. They hugged and decided to make up.

“I missed you too,” Nigar said. “Sit down.”

They drank tea and talked for hours. Nigar learned a good lesson. True friends can live far away, but they never leave your heart.

B1.text:
When Nigar and Aysel met at university in Baku five years ago, they hit it off immediately. They shared all their secrets and spent every afternoon together. However, last year Aysel accepted a hotel management job in Sheki. This suddenly turned their close friendship into a long-distance relationship.

At first, they promised to video call every single weekend. But the new hotel was demanding, and Aysel started cancelling their chats. The first real conflict happened in November. Nigar was very upset because Aysel completely forgot her birthday.

“You only care about your job now!” Nigar shouted over the phone one Friday night.

Aysel got angry and defensive, saying she was just stressed. They hung up without saying goodbye. Over the next month, they began to drift apart. Nigar stopped sending funny pictures, and Aysel stopped replying to quick messages.

December in Baku was freezing cold. Nigar walked along the Boulevard, feeling a heavy sadness in her chest. She missed her best friend's advice and warm laughter. Sitting on a wooden bench, she finally opened her chat with Aysel. She started typing a message to apologize.

Before she could press the send button, she suddenly heard her name. She turned around and saw Aysel standing right behind her. Aysel was holding a small suitcase and a big box of Sheki pakhlava.

“I took two days off from the hotel,” Aysel said, looking nervous. “I know I was a terrible friend recently. Can we start again?”

Nigar felt tears in her eyes. “Of course we can,” she smiled. “But you are buying the coffee today.”

They spent the whole weekend walking around Icherisheher, talking and laughing just like the old days. It wasn't easy to fix everything in one day, but they knew their bond was much stronger than the miles between them.

B2.text:
When Nigar and Aysel crossed paths during their freshman year at Baku State University, they hit it off instantly. For years, they were inseparable. Nigar deeply valued Aysel’s unwavering loyalty; she was the kind of friend who would stand by someone through any crisis. However, their dynamic was severely tested when Aysel relocated to Sheki to manage a boutique hotel.

Maintaining a long-distance friendship proved harder than either had anticipated. The physical distance wasn't the main issue—it was the conflicting schedules. Aysel was constantly overwhelmed with guests, frequently cancelling their planned catch-ups. The tension finally boiled over into a bitter conflict the week of Nigar’s promotion. Aysel forgot to call, and Nigar felt completely abandoned.

“You’re so wrapped up in your career that you’ve forgotten I exist!” Nigar snapped during a brief, tense phone call. Aysel responded defensively, claiming she was just trying to survive her first year in management, and for the first time, they hung up in anger.

Weeks passed in stubborn silence. They began to drift apart, becoming little more than passive viewers of each other’s social media stories. Without their daily chats, Nigar felt a distinct void in her routine.

One freezing December evening, Nigar was wandering aimlessly along the Boulevard, wrapping her scarf tighter against the biting Caspian wind. She missed Aysel terribly. Realising her own pride was getting in the way, she pulled out her phone to draft an apology.

Just as her thumb hovered over the screen, a familiar voice called out. Nigar spun around to find Aysel shivering by a bench, clutching a travel bag and a recognizable box of Sheki sweets.

“I caught the earliest bus I could,” Aysel said, her voice shaking slightly. “I’m so sorry I wasn’t there to celebrate your promotion. I was a terrible friend.”

Nigar’s frustration melted instantly. “I shouldn't have yelled at you,” she admitted, pulling Aysel into a tight embrace.

Over a steaming pot of thyme tea at a nearby cafe, they reached a much-needed compromise. Aysel promised to block out Sunday mornings exclusively for Nigar, and Nigar agreed to be more understanding of hotel emergencies. They realised that true friendship requires effort, and neither was willing to let the other go.

podcast.title: A pencil for an apple

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Who is your oldest friend? Guess: whose best friend lives in Canada now — Leyla's or Sam's?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is friendship. Leyla, how did you meet your best friend?
On the first day of school. We were six. She took my pencil, and I took her apple.
[laugh] A fair trade.
We hit it off immediately. Twenty-five years later, she's still my best friend. But now she lives in Canada.
Oh, so it's a long-distance friendship.
Yes. There's a nine-hour time difference. When I wake up, she's going to bed.
How do you keep it strong?
Every Sunday morning we have a video call. Sometimes it's two hours. And she always remembers my exams, my interviews, everything. She's so supportive.
That's loyalty. I'm a bit jealous. I had a best friend at school too — Danny. But after university we started to drift apart.
What happened?
Nothing big. No conflict, no fight. He moved to another city, got married, and we just… stopped calling.
[sigh] That happens to many people. It's sad, but it's normal.
Last month I sent him a message. We talked for an hour, like in the old days.
That's lovely! And do you and your friends ever argue?
Of course. My flatmate and I argue about the dishes every week.
[chuckle] And then you make up?
Always. We found a compromise — I cook, and he washes up.
For me, the most important thing is trust. I can tell my friend anything, and it stays between us.
Agreed. And a real friend will stand by someone even when they make a mistake.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: who is your oldest friend — and how did you meet?
Mine is Danny. I think I'll call him again. See you next time!
Bye for now!
